# Jeremiah 13 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Overview

The chapter consists of five sections: (1) the acted parable of the linen loincloth (vv. 1–11), (2) the parable of the wine jars (vv. 12–14), (3) a warning against pride (vv. 15–17), (4) an address to the king and queen mother (vv. 18–19), and (5) a lament over Jerusalem's coming shame (vv. 20–27). The chapter may be a compilation of several prophecies delivered at different times (Enduring Word). Ellicott dates it to the brief three-month reign of Jehoiachin (c. 597 BC), based on the reference to the queen mother in v. 18. The Cambridge Bible notes the first two sections are in poetic prose and the remainder in *qinah* (lament) metre.

**Sources used throughout:** Enduring Word (David Guzik) at enduringword.com; Ellicott's Commentary at biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges at biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm; Pulpit Commentary at biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/13.htm; The Gospel Coalition (TGC) at thegospelcoalition.org; search excerpts from Calvin, Clarke, Haydock, Expositor's, and Garner-Howes.

---

## Part 1: The Linen Loincloth (vv. 1–11)

### v. 1 — "Go and buy yourself a linen loincloth..."

**The material and its significance.** The loincloth (or "girdle" in older translations) was made of linen, the material appointed for priestly garments (Exodus 28:42; Leviticus 16:4). This made it the fittest material to symbolize the people of God, who were called to be "a kingdom of priests" (Cambridge Bible). Ellicott adds that of all garments, the girdle was nearest to the wearer's body and most identified with his activity — a fitting picture of Israel's closeness to Jehovah. The word "buy" (or "get") implies a purchase, which itself carried symbolic weight (Ellicott). Guzik (Enduring Word) notes the linen belt was "a sign of dignity and nobility," associated with both the High Priest and wealthy nobles.

**"Do not let it touch water."** Several interpretations are offered:
- Ellicott: The unwashed girdle represented the guilt of the people unpurified by any real contact with the "clean water" of repentance (cf. Ezekiel 36:25; Zechariah 3:3). The normal priestly work involved frequent washings; the command was exceptional.
- Cambridge Bible: Jeremiah was not to soften the garment for comfort, or more significantly, to keep it separate from what would cause it to be marred — thus symbolizing Israel in its earlier independence and the sunshine of Jehovah's favour.
- Pulpit (citing Jerome): It symbolized the character of the people — stiff and impure like unwashed linen.

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/13.htm

### v. 2 — "So I bought a loincloth..."

Jeremiah's immediate obedience is noted. The narrative is presented as a straightforward historical report, not a vision. Ellicott insists "there are absolutely no grounds whatever for looking upon it as a vision or a parable."

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm

### vv. 3–4 — "Take the loincloth... go at once to Perath and hide it there..."

**Where is "Perath"?** This is one of the most debated questions in the chapter. The Hebrew word is the same as "Euphrates" everywhere else in the OT. The options are:

1. **The literal Euphrates River** (Ellicott, Guzik, G.A. Smith cited in Cambridge). This would require a double journey of 250–400 miles each way. Ellicott defends it vigorously: the command given by Nebuchadnezzar in Jeremiah's favour (Jer 39:11) "implies some previous knowledge which may reasonably be connected with this visit." Guzik notes the Euphrates was the direction from which future conquerors would come. Morgan (cited by Guzik) says, "Personally, I believe that it is history, that Jeremiah actually travelled to Babylon and back twice." If literal, the rocky cleft would be in the upper Euphrates (above Carchemish), since the lower river flows through an alluvial plain (Cambridge).

2. **Parah (Wady Fara), near Anathoth** (Joshua 18:23), about 3 miles NE of Jeremiah's hometown. The name resembles Perath and the location has rocky gorges with a stream. Supported by Ewald and Birch (cited in Pulpit).

3. **Ephrath (Bethlehem)** — Bochart's view, adopted by the Pulpit Commentary. The limestone hills of this region provided abundant secluded rocks. The Pulpit prefers this to avoid the geographical difficulties.

4. **A vision or subjective experience** (Cambridge Bible leans here). "It is more natural to consider that the transaction was of a subjective character, taking place in the prophet's mind only."

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/13.htm

### vv. 5–7 — The burial, long interval, and retrieval

**"Many days later."** Ellicott suggests the interval may have been around seventy days — long enough to be an "adequate symbol of the seventy years' exile" — though the text does not specify. The Cambridge Bible says the interval was simply long enough for the cloth to rot.

**"It was ruined — of no use at all."** The loincloth had deteriorated from moisture and dirt. It still existed, but was "profitable for nothing." Guzik notes it "had nothing of the previous nobility and prominence that it once displayed." The Cambridge Bible adds that the prophet's action (burying) represents Jehovah, and the action by which the girdle's beauty is destroyed "corresponds thus to exile... but not to apostasy" — the humbling, not the moral corruption, is what the symbol primarily represents. Ellicott says the ruined girdle was "a parable of the state of Judah after the exile, stripped of all its outward greatness."

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm

### vv. 8–11 — The interpretation: ruined pride

**v. 9 — "I will ruin the pride of Judah and the great pride of Jerusalem."** The girdle was the part of dress on which most ornamental work was lavished, a common gift among princes (1 Samuel 18:4; 2 Samuel 18:11), making it a natural symbol of outward glory (Ellicott). The "great pride" or "gross pride" of Jerusalem would be destroyed just as the girdle was spoiled (Thompson, cited by Guzik).

**v. 10 — "These evil people, who refuse to listen to My words..."** Three sins are enumerated: (1) refusing to hear God's words, (2) following the stubbornness of their own hearts, (3) going after other gods. Guzik notes the progression: when they stopped listening to God and started following their own hearts, it led inevitably to idolatry. They would become "like this loincloth — of no use at all." The Cambridge Bible notes that some critics (Cornill) thought vv. 9 and 10–11 gave two mutually exclusive explanations, but the Cambridge editors argue the exile (v. 9) is the humbling and the apostasy (v. 10) is its cause — there is no real inconsistency.

**v. 11 — "As a loincloth clings to a man's waist, so I have made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to Me."** This is the heart of the parable. God had bound Israel to Himself in the closest intimacy, "that they might be My people for My renown and praise and glory" (cf. Deuteronomy 26:19). Guzik elaborates: "Just as a fine sash expressed beauty and nobility, so God wanted His people to be ornaments of His greatness to all the world." Ryken (cited by Guzik) says, "The chief purpose and ultimate goal of human beings is to be wrapped around God's waist like a fashion accessory. When we are at our very best, we adorn God with glory."

The Cambridge Bible notes the phrase "the whole house of Israel and" may be a later gloss (based on the Syriac Hexapla), but Ellicott sees it as evidence that the prophet's sense of national unity was still strong — not just Judah but all Israel had been Jehovah's girdle.

**"But they did not listen."** Despite their high calling, the people's stubborn and persistent sins made them useless and ruined (Guzik). The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary (search excerpt) emphasizes that God "has chosen and designed His covenant people for a walk of intimacy with Himself" and desires this nearness so that they may be "a name for Himself," show forth His praise, and glorify His name among the nations.

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-13.html

## Part 2: The Wine Jars (vv. 12–14)

### v. 12 — "Every wineskin shall be filled with wine"

**A proverb turned on its head.** The saying "every bottle (jar) shall be filled with wine" was a popular proverb. Kidner (cited by Guzik) says it meant something optimistic like "the more you expect, the more you'll get" or "it'll all come right in the end." The people would reply with a shrug — "Don't we surely know that?" — treating Jeremiah's word as a truism. The "bottle" (Hebrew *nebel*) was the largest earthenware container for storing wine, not a skin (Ellicott, Harrison cited by Guzik, Cambridge).

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm

### vv. 13–14 — "I am going to fill with drunkenness all who live in this land..."

**God's twist.** Instead of wine filling jars to fulfill their purpose, God would fill the people with "drunkenness" — the wine of His wrath causing confusion, stupor, and helplessness (cf. Psalm 60:3; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). The Cambridge Bible says, "Through Jehovah's judicial action they are paralysed mentally, as with strong drink, and thus made to collide to their destruction."

All ranks are included: kings "who sit on David's throne" (Ellicott notes the plural refers to the four kings — Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah — all involved in the coming disaster), priests, prophets, and all inhabitants.

**"I will smash them against one another, fathers and sons alike."** The image shifts from filling to smashing. The Pulpit Commentary clarifies this is "merely the development of the figure of the pitchers; not a prediction of civil war." As earthen jars dashed together shatter, so God would destroy His people. The Cambridge Bible adds that the smashing "shall be of the most harrowing description" — fathers and sons together. God declares He will show "no mercy or pity or compassion."

The TGC commentary (thegospelcoalition.org) notes that sign-acts were "special actions that prophets perform to illustrate their message," and this second sign-act follows the loincloth to reinforce the warning.

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/13.htm; thegospelcoalition.org

## Part 3: Warning Against Pride (vv. 15–17)

### v. 15 — "Listen and give heed. Do not be arrogant, for the LORD has spoken."

The exhortation is direct. Ellicott notes that "be not proud" has "special reference to the besetting sin of Judah, as described in Jeremiah 13:9; perhaps also to the character of the symbols applied — the marred girdle and the broken jar — as being in themselves humiliating, and therefore a trial to their pride." The Cambridge Bible paraphrases: "Do not refuse through self-sufficiency to listen."

— biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm

### v. 16 — "Give glory to the LORD your God before He brings darkness..."

**"Give glory to the LORD."** This phrase carries a specific sense here: confessing sin and submitting to God's authority. Ellicott compares it to Joshua 7:19 ("My son, give glory to the LORD... and tell me what you have done") and John 9:24 — it means confessing the truth, even when that truth is a sin that involves punishment. The Cambridge Bible similarly says "by confession of sin and obedience." Calvin (in the search excerpt) explains: "To give glory to God is the same as to ascribe to him what properly belongs to him, or to acknowledge his power so as to be submissive to his word... Whosoever then does not fear and reverence God, whosoever does not believe his word, he robs him of his glory."

**"Before He brings darkness, before your feet stumble on the dusky mountains."** The image is of mountain travellers overtaken by deepening twilight who wait hopefully for dawn, but instead of light, deeper gloom descends (Cambridge). "Mountains of twilight" (*harere nesheph*) is a vivid poetic phrase — the dusk deepens into the midnight "shadow of death" (Ellicott, Cambridge). The Pulpit Commentary adds that a "mountain" in Scripture imagery represents a great obstacle (Zechariah 4:7; Matthew 21:21); Judah's previously smooth path would give way to huge mountains wrapped in impenetrable dusk.

Guzik urges the urgency: "there was still time to humble themselves and give glory to God before the darkness came, but they refused."

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/13.htm; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-13.html

### v. 17 — "But if you do not listen, I will weep in secret because of your pride."

**Jeremiah's tears.** This verse reveals the prophet's tender heart. Ellicott calls it "exquisite tenderness as characteristic of the prophet's temperament," comparing it to the tears of Jesus over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41) and Paul's "great heaviness and continual sorrow" (Romans 9:2). The "secret places" suggest silent, solitary grief and intercession — like Jesus withdrawing to a "solitary place" (Mark 1:35). The Cambridge Bible says Jeremiah "will in silent grief witness your ruin."

The reason for tears: "because the LORD's flock has been taken captive." The people are Jehovah's flock, and the rulers elsewhere called "shepherds" (Cambridge). Guzik adds: "Good ministers should be full of compassionate tears, weeping in secret for their people's unprofitableness, and their danger thereby" (Trapp).

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm

## Part 4: Address to the Royal House (vv. 18–19)

### v. 18 — "Say to the king and to the queen mother: 'Take a lowly seat...'"

**The royal figures.** The "queen" (Hebrew *gebirah*, "mistress" or "great lady") is the queen mother, not the king's wife. In the oriental court the queen mother held great influence (Pulpit, Cambridge). Ellicott identifies her as Nehushta, mother of the young King Jehoiachin (2 Kings 24:8), who reigned only three months before being taken captive to Babylon. The Cambridge Bible notes that most scholars agree with this identification, making the prophecy around 597 BC. The prominence of the queen mother was enhanced by the king's youth.

**"Take a lowly seat, for your glorious crowns have fallen from your heads."** Literally "sit down low" — take the posture of mourners or the humbled. The Pulpit Commentary says, "take the station suitable for your abased circumstances" (cf. Isaiah 47:1). The Cambridge Bible, following the LXX, renders: "for come down from your head is your beautiful crown." Feinberg (cited by Guzik) notes, "Pride was characteristic of the royal house."

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/13.htm

### v. 19 — "The cities of the Negev have been shut tight... All Judah has been carried into exile."

**Prophetic perfect tense.** The Hebrew uses the perfect tense — describing future events as if already accomplished, "the tense of prophetic certitude" (Pulpit). The Negev (the dry southern region of Judah) is specified to show that even the most remote areas would not escape the invader (Cambridge). Ellicott explains Nebuchadnezzar's strategy: blockade the southern cities, then attack Jerusalem.

"All Judah has been carried into exile, wholly taken captive" — Feinberg (cited by Guzik) notes this is "rhetorical exaggeration, since only some leaders and skilled workmen were taken to Babylon at that time (597 BC). Yet they represented the whole nation." The Cambridge Bible, following the LXX, suggests "an entire captivity."

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/13.htm

---

## Part 5: Jerusalem's Shame and Inability to Change (vv. 20–27)

### v. 20 — "Lift up your eyes and see those coming from the north."

The Hebrew verbs are feminine singular, so the address is to the personified city of Jerusalem ("daughter of Zion") (Thompson cited by Guzik, Cambridge). The invaders "from the north" are the Babylonians (and possibly their Scythian allies), the recurring threat in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:14; 4:6; 6:1, 22).

**"Where is the flock entrusted to you, the sheep that were your pride?"** Jerusalem, as the capital and "shepherd" of the nation, is asked to account for the people under her care. The "beautiful flock" had been committed to her stewardship (Ellicott).

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm

### v. 21 — "What will you say when He sets over you close allies whom you yourself trained?"

**The betrayal of former friends.** The meaning is difficult but the general sense is clear: those whom Judah had courted as allies (Babylon and perhaps lesser neighbouring nations) would now become her harsh masters. Ellicott translates: "What wilt thou say? for He (Jehovah) shall set over thee as head those whom thou taughtest to be thy familiar friends." The Cambridge Bible similarly renders: "What wilt thou say, when he shall set over thee as head those whom thou hast thyself taught to be friends unto thee?" The Pulpit Commentary paraphrases: Judah had trained these nations "to be captains" over her. The "pangs of anguish... like a woman in labor" would grip Jerusalem — the image of sudden, overwhelming, inescapable pain (Isaiah 13:8; 21:3).

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/13.htm

### v. 22 — "Why has this happened to me? ...your skirts have been stripped off and your body has been exposed."

**The shame of the adulteress.** Jerusalem would ask "why?" but the answer is clear — "because of the magnitude of your iniquity." The imagery of stripping off skirts and exposing the body is the public disgrace heaped on prostitutes (Feinberg cited by Guzik). Ellicott explains that the "skirts" or flowing train worn by women of rank would be removed — a sign of extremest degradation (Isaiah 20:4; 47:2; Ezekiel 23:29; Hosea 2:3; Nahum 3:5). "Thy heels made bare" is a euphemism — better rendered "body ravished" (Harrison cited by Guzik) or "treated with violence" (Pulpit). Kidner (cited by Guzik) summarizes: "A people that parts with its virtue — its morals, its integrity, its faith — will find itself not liberated, only cheapened: stripped of everything that gave it value and respect."

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/13.htm

### v. 23 — "Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?"

**The impossibility of self-reformation.** This is one of the most famous proverbs in Scripture. The Ethiopian (Cushite) was familiar to the Jews through Egyptian contact, and leopard-skins were associated with Ethiopian warriors (Ellicott, citing Herodotus). The Cambridge Bible clarifies that the verse "need not mean that Judah's sin was innate... but that habits of evil preclude a return to righteousness." Ellicott says the evil of Judah was "too deep-ingrained to be capable of spontaneous reformation. There remained nothing but the sharp discipline of the exile."

**Guzik's theological note (Pentecostal/charismatic perspective):** "Evil may be so ingrained in men that they find it impossible to change. Yet, especially from a broader Biblical perspective, we see the transforming work of Jesus Christ. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation... The Ethiopian cannot change his skin nor the leopard his spots; but the LORD God can transform men and women." He quotes Spurgeon: "The question of the text is, 'Can the Ethiopian change his skin?' The answer is, — No, no, no... Here is the other question, — Can the Ethiopian's skin be changed? The answer to that is, — Yes, yes, yes... Can the sinner's nature be renewed? Yes, for God can do everything."

**Catholic perspective (Haydock):** "Bad habits are a sort of second nature. I speak in vain. Yet God sometimes converts inveterate sinners, who cannot rise of themselves."

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-13.html

### vv. 24–25 — "I will scatter you like chaff driven by the desert wind."

The Hebrew word for "stubble" means the broken straw left on the threshing-floor after the oxen had trampled the corn — liable to be carried away by the first desert gale (Pulpit, citing Payne Smith; Ellicott). The "wind of the wilderness" is the scorching simoom from the Arabian desert (Jeremiah 4:11; Job 1:19). 

**"This is your lot, the portion I have measured to you."** The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew phrase "portion of thy measures" may refer to the upper garment used as a bag to hold something (Ruth 3:15; 2 Kings 4:39) — thus "the portion of thy garment" — punishment measured out into their lap.

**"Because you have forgotten Me and trusted in falsehood."** "Falsehood" means false gods (Jeremiah 16:19). The Pulpit Commentary adds: "The attachment of Judah to The Lie was in itself a great shame, an act of adultery" (Thompson).

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/13.htm

### vv. 26–27 — "So I will pull your skirts up over your face, that your shame may be seen."

**"I also" — divine retaliation.** The Pulpit notes the Hebrew "And I also" (not just "therefore") implies divine retaliation — a measured, fitting punishment (citing Calvin, cf. Proverbs 1:26; Nahum 3:5). Pulling skirts over the face is a graphic image of exposure and humiliation.

**"Your adulteries and lustful neighings, your shameless prostitution on the hills and in the fields."** The "neighings" (as in Jeremiah 2:24; 5:8) are a "bestial figure for illicit love" (Feinberg cited by Guzik), expressing the unbridled eagerness of animal passion transferred to spiritual idolatry (Ellicott, Pulpit). The "abominations on the hills" refer to the orgiastic rites of high-place worship, "in the field" emphasizing their public, shameless character (Ellicott).

**"Woe to you, O Jerusalem! How long will you remain unclean?"** The chapter ends not with finality but with a question that implies hope. Ellicott says tenderly: "Sad as the last words are, they in some measure soften the idea of irretrievable finality. 'Will the time ever come, and if so, when?' Like the cry addressed to God, 'How long, O Lord...' (Revelation 6:10), it implies a hope, though only just short of despair." The Pulpit Commentary agrees: Jeremiah "cannot continue to hold such gloomy thoughts; surely Israel, God's people, must eventually be 'made clean!' But this can only be as the result of judicial affliction." The Cambridge Bible renders it: "How long will it be, ere thou be made clean?"

— enduringword.com; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/jeremiah/13.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/13.htm

---

## Tradition-Specific Emphases

### Reformed (Calvin)
On v. 16, Calvin stresses that "giving glory to God" means acknowledging His power and submitting to His word. All unbelievers "rob him of his glory" even while professing otherwise. The sovereignty of God in judgment and the necessity of humble submission to His revealed word are the dominant notes.
— studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-13.html (search excerpt)

### Baptist (Garner-Howes)
Emphasizes that God "has chosen and designed His covenant people for a walk of intimacy with Himself" (citing Exodus 19:5–6; Deuteronomy 7:6–11). The linen garment illustrates "the nearness of relationship that the Lord desires with His people." God's purposes are: to set His people forth before an unbelieving world, to make them a name for Himself, to show forth His praise, to glorify His name, and to be "a people for His own possession" (1 Peter 2:9).
— studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/jeremiah-13.html (search excerpt)

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (David Guzik, Enduring Word)
Guzik emphasizes the transforming power of Christ in connection with v. 23: though human nature cannot change itself, God can and does transform men and women through new creation in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17). The chapter is an urgent call to humble oneself before the Lord "before it's too late." Spurgeon is quoted at length on God's power to change the sinner's nature.
— enduringword.com

### Catholic (Haydock)
Notes that the girdle was "usually worn by women" (citing Jerome, contra Exodus 28:42). On v. 23, Haydock says "bad habits are a sort of second nature," yet "God sometimes converts inveterate sinners, who cannot rise of themselves." The commentary also notes the possibility that God could have transported Jeremiah to the Euphrates supernaturally (like Habakkuk to Daniel), though this is not necessary.
— studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-13.html (search excerpt)

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible / bible.org — search excerpt)
The NET Bible textual notes (as represented in the bible.org page) point out that the chapter contains both prose (vv. 1–14) and poetic sections (vv. 15–27). The UBS Handbook divides the poetic section into three strophes by content. The symbolic acts here are compared to similar acts by Isaiah (20:2–6), Ezekiel (chapters 4–5), and others. On the geography of Perath, modern scholarship tends to see the literal Euphrates as intended, since the point is that the loincloth was buried in a foreign land symbolizing exile.
— bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-13 (search excerpt)

### Evangelical (The Gospel Coalition)
Matthew Patton's TGC commentary notes that the chapter "develops the fury and grief of Yahweh concerning the pride of his beloved people." The loincloth illustrates "Yahweh's disappointment with his people. He had intended them for beauty and for glory... but instead of clinging to Yahweh, they buried themselves in foreign idolatry." The exhortation "Give glory to the Lord" (v. 16) "recalls Joshua's attempt to elicit a confession from Achan when he was clearly condemned (Josh 7:19)."
— thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/jeremiah/
